interpretation: After exact-point Thalassia loss, retaining another seagrass at the same meter mark is associated with a substantially higher probability of re-recording Thalassia one year later than transitioning to a no-seagrass state. This is consistent with habitat continuity rather than a simple alternative-state lock-in pattern.
ecological_boundary: The pattern can arise from shared favorable habitat, residual Thalassia rhizomes, microsite stability, or species interactions; it does not establish facilitation or demographic recolonization.
claim_boundary: Post-hoc derived ecological endpoint from an already-opened exact-point panel.
Return is re-recorded Thalassia at the same meter mark, not demographic recolonization.
Alternative-seagrass occupancy is a state marker and may not causally promote return.
Do not interpret the result as proof of facilitation or equivalent ecosystem function among species.
